name: Practice and dispassion (abhyāsa-vairāgya, YS 1.12)
summary: YS 1.12: the activities of the mind (vṛtti) are stilled by practice (abhyāsa) and dispassion (vairāgya). Vyāsa: the river of the mind flows both ways; dispassion dams the stream toward objects, and practice in discriminative seeing opens the stream toward discrimination. Practice is the effort toward stability, the calm flow of a mind without activities (1.13 with Vyāsa); it becomes firmly grounded when cultivated for a long time, without interruption and with devotion (1.14). Dispassion is the consciousness of mastery of one who is free of thirst for objects seen or heard of (1.15); Vyāsa: the mind sees the faults of objects by the strength of reflection.
steps: Sit in a posture that is steady and comfortable (YS 2.46).
Make the effort toward stability: let the mind settle into a calm flow (YS 1.13 with Vyāsa).
When the mind turns toward an object it thirsts for, seen or heard of, see the object's faults and let the thirst go (YS 1.15 with Vyāsa).
Return to the effort toward stability without strain; relax effort, as the sūtra says of posture (YS 2.47).
Close gently, and take the practice up again on the following days without interruption (YS 1.14).

name: Practice on a single principle (ekatattva-abhyāsa, YS 1.32)
summary: YS 1.32: to counter them (the distractions of 1.30 and their companions of 1.31) there is practice on a single principle. Vyāsa: to counter distraction the mind should practise resting on a single principle (ekatattvāvalambana); when the mind is drawn back from everything and concentrated on one object, it becomes one-pointed. Neither the sūtra nor this gloss names the object.

Choose one object and let the mind rest on it alone (YS 1.32 with Vyāsa: ekatattvāvalambana).
When the mind goes to other things, draw it back from them and set it again on the one object (Vyāsa on 1.32).
Keep the effort light: the effort toward stability is itself the practice (YS 1.13).
Close gently.

name: The yoga of action: austerity, self-study, devotion to Īśvara (kriyā-yoga, YS 2.1)
summary: YS 2.1: austerity (tapas), self-study (svādhyāya) and devotion to Īśvara (īśvara-praṇidhāna) are the yoga of action. YS 2.2: it is for cultivating samādhi and for thinning the afflictions (kleśa). Vyāsa: yoga does not succeed for one without austerity; self-study is the repetition of purifying words such as Oṃ or the study of texts on liberation; devotion to Īśvara is offering all actions to the supreme teacher, or renouncing their fruit. Vyāsa introduces it as the yoga for one whose mind is not yet concentrated.

name: Meditation that abandons the afflictions' activities (dhyāna, YS 2.11)
summary: YS 2.11: the activities (vṛtti) of the afflictions are to be abandoned by meditation (dhyāna). Vyāsa: the gross activities, first thinned by kriyā-yoga, are abandoned by reflection (prasaṃkhyāna), by meditation, until they are made subtle like burnt seeds; as the gross dirt of cloth is shaken off first and the fine dirt removed afterwards with effort and means, so the gross activities have small opponents and the subtle ones great opponents.

name: Cultivating the opposite (pratipakṣa-bhāvanā, YS 2.33–34)
summary: YS 2.33: when one is oppressed by harmful thoughts (vitarka), one should cultivate their opposites. YS 2.34: harmful thoughts such as violence, whether done, caused to be done or approved, preceded by greed, anger or delusion, mild, middling or intense, have endless suffering and ignorance as their fruit; reflecting thus is the cultivation of the opposite. Vyāsa gives the yogin's reflection: having taken refuge in yoga, to take back the harmful thoughts one has given up would be like a dog returning to its vomit. The restraints the harmful thoughts oppose are non-harming, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy and non-possessiveness (2.30). Vyāsa on 2.4: afflictions struck down by the cultivation of the opposite become thin (tanu).
steps: Sit in a posture that is steady and comfortable (YS 2.46).
When a harmful thought arises, to harm, to lie, to take what is not given, name it as a harmful thought (vitarka) (YS 2.33 with Vyāsa).
See how it stands: done, caused to be done, or approved; rooted in greed, anger or delusion; mild, middling or intense (YS 2.34).
Reflect that such thoughts bear endless suffering and ignorance as their fruit (YS 2.34).
Turn the mind toward the restraint the thought opposes, such as non-harming or truthfulness (YS 2.33; 2.30).
Close gently.

name: Neither attachment nor pride when invited by the high ones (YS 3.51)

name: Practice and dispassion (abhyāsa, vairāgya, BhG 6.35)
summary: BhG 6.34–35: Arjuna says the mind is restless, turbulent, strong and obstinate, as hard to restrain as the wind; Kṛṣṇa answers that the mind is without doubt hard to restrain and restless, but it is held by practice (abhyāsa) and dispassion (vairāgya). 6.36: yoga is hard to attain for one whose self is unrestrained, but one whose self is under control and who strives can attain it through the right means.

name: The embodied one and the body (BhG 2.11–30)
summary: BhG 2.11–30: Kṛṣṇa's first teaching to the grieving Arjuna. The wise grieve neither for those whose life has gone nor for those whose life has not gone (2.11); as the embodied one passes through childhood, youth and old age, so it attains another body (2.13); the contacts of the senses come and go, endure them (2.14); of what is not there is no being, of what is there is no non-being (2.16); the embodied one is unborn, eternal, not slain when the body is slain (2.20); therefore one ought not to grieve for any beings (2.30).

name: Telling the good from the pleasant (śreyas and preyas, KU 1.2.1–2)
summary: KU 1.2.1–2: the good (śreyas) is one thing, the pleasant (preyas) another; both bind a person with different aims. Good comes to one who takes the good; one who chooses the pleasant misses the goal. Both come to a person; the wise one examines them all round and distinguishes them; the wise prefers the good to the pleasant, the dull one chooses the pleasant for the sake of getting and keeping (yoga-kṣema).

Notice where the pull is 'for the sake of getting and keeping' (yoga-kṣema) (1.2.2).

summary: TU 3.1.1: Bhṛgu Vāruṇi approached his father Varuṇa: 'Sir, teach me brahman.' name: Meditation on Oṃ and its measures (MāU 8–12)

name: Acting with situational awareness (sampajañña, MN 10:8)
summary: MN 10:8: a mendicant acts with situational awareness when going out and coming back; when looking ahead and aside; when bending and extending the limbs; when bearing robe and bowl; when eating, drinking, chewing and tasting; when urinating and defecating; when walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking and keeping silent. name: Observing the mind (cittānupassanā, MN 10:34)
summary: MN 10:34 (and DN 22:12): a mendicant understands mind with greed as 'mind with greed' and mind without greed as 'mind without greed'; likewise mind with and without hate, with and without delusion; constricted and scattered mind; expansive and unexpansive; not supreme and supreme; immersed and not immersed in samādhi; freed and unfreed. Close gently.

name: Observing the five hindrances (MN 10:36)
summary: MN 10:36 (and DN 22:13): when sensual desire is in them, a mendicant understands 'I have sensual desire in me'; when it is not, they understand 'I don't have sensual desire in me'. name: Observing the four noble truths (MN 10:44; DN 22:17–21)

name: Mindfulness of breathing, first tetrad (MN 118:17–18)
summary: MN 118:17–18: gone to a wilderness, the root of a tree or an empty hut, a mendicant sits down cross-legged, sets the body straight and brings mindfulness to the present. Just mindful, they breathe in; mindful, they breathe out. Breathing in heavily (long) they know it; breathing in lightly (short) they know it; likewise breathing out. They train: 'I'll breathe in and out experiencing the whole body'; 'I'll breathe in and out stilling the bodily process.' Developed and cultivated, mindfulness of breathing fulfils the four kinds of mindfulness meditation (118:15).
steps: Sit comfortably with the body straight, and bring mindfulness to the present (MN 118:17; the text has cross-legged).
Just mindful, breathe in; mindful, breathe out. Let the breath be as it is; the sutta only asks that you know it (MN 118:17).
Breathing in long, know 'I breathe in long'; breathing in short, know 'I breathe in short'; likewise breathing out (MN 118:18).
Train: 'I'll breathe in and out experiencing the whole body' (MN 118:18).
Close gently.

tier_reason: Knowing the natural breath, as the sutta's first steps ask; no counting, retention or forcing. The Visuddhimagga calls this subject weighty and asks for strong mindfulness (Vism VIII, PTS p.284), so the steps stop before the fourth step.

name: Perceiving light against dullness and drowsiness (DN 2:68)
summary: DN 2:68: giving up dullness and drowsiness, one meditates with a mind rid of dullness and drowsiness, perceiving light (āloka-saññī), mindful and aware, cleansing the mind of dullness and drowsiness. It stands in the sutta's account of giving up the five hindrances, after ethics, sense restraint, mindfulness and contentment, with the practitioner seated, body straight, mindfulness brought to the present (DN 2:67).
steps: Sit with the body straight and bring mindfulness to the present (DN 2:67).
Give attention to the perception of light (āloka-saññā) (DN 2:68).
Stay mindful and aware (sato sampajāno) (DN 2:68).
Let the mind be cleansed of dullness and drowsiness in this way (DN 2:68).

tier_reason: Attention to the perception of light while mindful; no breath control, fasting or austerity.

name: Developing loving-kindness (mettā-bhāvanā, Vism IX)
summary: Dhp 5: hatred is never laid to rest by hate; it is laid to rest by non-hatred; this is an ancient teaching. Vism IX: the beginner, in a secluded place, seated comfortably, first reviews the danger in hate and the advantage in patience (p.295); begins with himself as the example, 'May I be happy and free from suffering', since as he wants happiness and shrinks from pain so do other beings (p.296–297); then extends it to a respected, dear person, then to a very dear friend, a neutral person and a hostile person, making the mind soft and workable toward each before going on (p.297). Mettā's mark is promoting welfare; it succeeds when ill will subsides (p.318).
steps: Sit comfortably in a quiet place (Vism IX p.295).
First consider the danger in hate and the advantage in patience (p.295).
Begin with yourself as the example: 'May I be happy and free from suffering'; as you want happiness and shrink from pain, so do others (p.296–297).
Extend the same wish to a person you respect and hold dear: 'May this good person be happy and free from suffering' (p.297).
Then, one by one, to a very dear friend, a neutral person and a hostile person, letting the mind grow soft toward each before moving on (p.297).
Close gently.

warnings.text: Do not begin with a disliked person, a very dear friend, a neutral person or an enemy; do not develop it specifically toward the opposite sex, nor toward the dead.
If resentment arises when the hostile person is brought to mind, go back to the earlier persons, enter mettā again and again, and return to that person repeatedly.
Mettā fails when selfish affection (sineha) arises; greed is its near enemy and ill will its far enemy.

tier_reason: Kindness developed in reflection, sitting quietly; no breath control, fasting or austerity.

name: Developing the divine abidings (brahmavihāra, Vism IX)
summary: Vism IX sets out loving-kindness (mettā), compassion (karuṇā), gladness (muditā) and equanimity (upekkhā). Mettā begins with oneself as the example and goes on to a dear, a very dear, a neutral and a hostile person (p.296–297). Compassion begins with someone seen in misfortune (p.314); gladness with a very dear companion, or a dear person seen or heard to be happy (p.316). Each has a mark, a near enemy and a far enemy (p.318–319). Vism III gives the four divine abidings as suited to the hate temperament (p.114).
steps: Sit comfortably in a quiet place (Vism IX p.295).
Mettā: begin with yourself as the example, then a respected person, a dear friend, a neutral person and a hostile person: 'May they be happy and free from suffering' (p.296–297).
Compassion (karuṇā): bring to mind someone in misfortune and hardship, and let compassion arise toward them (p.314).
Gladness (muditā): bring to mind a dear person seen or heard to be happy, and rejoice: 'How glad this being is!' (p.316).
Close gently.

warnings.text: Equanimity (upekkhā) and the formless states are not to be taken up by a beginner.
For compassion and gladness, as for mettā, a person of the opposite sex and the dead are 'not the field' (akhetta).
The Vism's first object for compassion is a destitute person in great hardship, described in bodily detail; the steps keep only 'someone in misfortune'.
Each abiding has its failure: selfish affection for mettā, sorrow for compassion, merriment for gladness; the near enemies are greed, worldly grief and worldly joy.

tier_reason: Kindness, compassion and gladness developed in reflection; equanimity is left out because Vism III says it is not for the beginner.

name: The six recollections (Vism VII)
summary: Vism VII describes six recollections: of the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, one's own virtue, one's own generosity, and the deities, with the deities as witnesses to one's own faith and other qualities (p.197). For the Buddha: one with firm confidence, gone into a suitable secluded place, recollects his qualities: 'That Blessed One is accomplished, fully enlightened, endowed with clear vision and virtuous conduct, sublime, knower of worlds, incomparable leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened and blessed', going through them one by one with the reason for each (p.198).

Recall the Buddha's qualities with the traditional words: 'That Blessed One is accomplished, fully enlightened, endowed with clear vision and virtuous conduct, sublime, knower of worlds, incomparable leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened and blessed' (p.198).

Close gently.
